sections.html:
Find the Register of Deeds inside the Chowan County courthouse, 101 S. Broad Street, Edenton. The mailing box is PO Box 487, Edenton, NC 27932. Call (252) 482-2619 or fax (252) 482-3062. Counter hours: eight to five, Monday through Friday.

Its mission statement names it the keeper of vital records and real estate recordings. Its real estate archive reaches back to the 1600s, marriage licenses are dated as early as 1868, and birth and death records start in 1913. That depth means a title search here can run through very old deeds.

The county has about 14,082 residents and 7,312 housing units. Median home value for 2020 to 2024 came to $235,800, with 70.5% of units lived in by their owners. Only 48 building permits were issued in 2025, so nearly every deed filed here moves an existing house or a parcel of land.

sections.h2: Checklist before a deed is recorded
sections.html:
Chowan adds a local land transfer tax, a parcel number approval and a stop at the tax office to the usual recording steps. Run down this list first.

Pre-recording checklist, Edenton office
RequirementWhat the office expects
Notary acknowledgmentSignature, seal and expiration date of the notary all filled in
Grantee addressPermanent mailing address printed on the deed itself
DrafterName of whoever drafted a deed or deed of trust, shown on page one
Recording feesPaid under the county fee list
Land transfer tax1% of the sale price, citing S.L. 1985-881
Excise tax$2.00 per $1,000 or fraction of it, based on the sales price
Parcel numberApproved by the Land Records/GIS Department for any document with a legal description
Tax officeDeed presented with an affidavit of consideration before recording

Every document needs a date and a legal description too. A deed with an attached survey, and any other survey, must be reviewed and signed by the county's review officer before it is recorded.

sections.h2: County land transfer tax and state excise tax
sections.html:
Sellers here owe two taxes. Edenton collects a 1% land transfer tax on the sale price (S.L. 1985-881) in addition to the state excise tax. In the statute, G.S. 105-228.30, the excise tax reads $1.00 per $500, and the county's list restates it as $2.00 per $1,000. Whoever transfers the property pays before the deed goes on record.

Both charges rise with the price, so skip guessing from memory. Ask the register or your closing attorney for today's numbers and for how your contract splits them. Neither tax can be put off until after recording. Read each tax line on your net sheet before you accept it.

sections.h2: Stops before the register of deeds
sections.html:
Two other offices handle a deed before the register does. Land Records/GIS approves a parcel identification number for any real estate document carrying a legal description, plats included, and its review officer signs surveys. Find it in the same courthouse at 101 S. Broad Street, or call (252) 482-7157.

The Tax Office is the second stop, and many sellers overlook it. The register will not record a deed until it has been shown there with an affidavit of consideration. The tax office is at 305 W. Freemason Street, Edenton, phone (252) 482-8486, mailing address PO Box 1030.

  1. An attorney prepares the deed, listing the drafter, the buyer's mailing address and the legal description.
  2. Land Records/GIS approves the parcel number and reviews any attached survey.
  3. Take the deed and the affidavit of consideration to the tax office.
  4. Pay the recording fee, excise tax and transfer tax at the register, and the deed is recorded.

A closing attorney normally runs all four. Without one, for instance when deeding a house to a relative, you carry out each step yourself.

Electronic recording in Edenton is limited to satisfactions, the papers that release a paid-off mortgage or deed of trust. Lenders and title companies send those online. Deeds, deeds of trust and plats, including the deed that sells your house, are delivered in person or mailed with the right fee.

Certified copies can be bought online by card for pickup or mail, and checkout adds a small processing fee. Staff will not help you complete documents or search title, since state law prohibits them from practicing law without a license.

The statewide schedule in G.S. 161-10 puts a general instrument at $26.00 through 15 pages and a deed of trust at $64.00 through 35, plus $4.00 per page beyond. Chowan's posted fee list controls, so phone ahead before writing a check.

sections.h2: What to bring to the counter
sections.html:
Recording without an attorney takes preparation. Carry the signed, notarized original with the drafter named on page one, a permanent mailing address for the buyer, a full legal description and a parcel number that Land Records/GIS has already approved. Add the affidavit of consideration from the tax office and money for the recording fee and both taxes.

Leave one item out and you probably make a second trip, since deeds cannot be e-recorded here. Staff can explain the fees but cannot repair a drafting mistake.

sections.h2: Property tax relief and a sale
sections.html:
Three state programs lower or defer tax for qualifying owners. You claim each one from the county assessor, not the Department of Revenue.

  • Senior and disabled owners may exclude whichever is greater, $25,000 or half the appraised value of a primary home, if 2026 income is $38,800 or less.
  • Owners with a disabled-veteran designation, and their unmarried surviving spouses, get $45,000 of appraised value excluded, with no age or income limit on the state form.
  • A circuit breaker limits the bill to a share of income and defers the rest as a lien that comes due on a sale or at the owner's death.

The deferral is what shows up at closing: tax deferred for up to three earlier years is payable once a disqualifying event, such as a sale, happens. See G.S. 105-277.1B, for the rules; the AV-9 application goes to the county tax office.

An unregistered deed offers little protection. Under G.S. 47-18, it affects purchasers and lien creditors only once registered where the land lies, and generally the earlier registration prevails. Both sides therefore want the deed filed the day of closing.

Property tax is the other thing to watch. Bills fall due September 1 and accrue interest after January 5 under G.S. 105-360, and the lien attaches to the parcel as of the listing date. Call the Tax Office, (252) 482-8486, for what you owe today, when the next revaluation is, and which relief programs apply to the house.

If you inherited a Chowan house, have fallen behind on payments or want to skip repairs, our North Carolina page describes a cash sale route. A cash buyer does not shortcut the process. The checklist, the tax office visit and the transfer tax still apply, so leave time before closing.

faqs.q: What number do I call for Chowan deed questions?
faqs.a: Call (252) 482-2619. The courthouse office at 101 S. Broad Street, Edenton, serves the public weekdays from 8:00 to 5:00.
No. The office e-records satisfactions only, so a deed must be mailed or delivered to Edenton with the correct fee.

faqs.q: What taxes apply when a Chowan deed is recorded?
faqs.a: A land transfer tax of 1% of the sale price and an excise tax of $2.00 per $1,000 or fraction. Both must be paid before recording.

faqs.q: Do I have to visit the tax office before recording in Chowan County?
faqs.a: Yes. Every deed goes to the Chowan County Tax Office with an affidavit of consideration first. The office is at 305 W. Freemason Street, Edenton.

faqs.q: Can Chowan County staff help me write or fix my deed?
faqs.a: No. They cannot help complete documents or do a title search, since that would be unauthorized practice of law. Use a North Carolina attorney.
